title.en: The Four Words of Wrong: Whiskey, Witchcraft, Poison, and the Cut String
title.zh: 四大惡言：烈酒、巫術、秘毒與斷絕

region.en: Cold Spring on the Allegany, Seneca country (where the message was first preached)
region.zh: 阿利根尼的冷泉，塞內卡之地（此訓示首次宣講處）

texts.period: Gai'wiio' (Code of Handsome Lake), recited 1800-1815, recorded by A. C. Parker 1913 (Sections 1-4)

source.work: A. C. Parker (ed.), The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet, NY State Museum Bulletin 163 (1913), Sections 1-4

summary.en: Four words tell a great story of wrong and the Creator is sad because of the trouble they bring. The first word is One'ga' - whiskey: the Creator made it and gave it to the white man as a medicine, 'but they use it for evil... No, the Creator did not make it for you.' The second word is Got'gon - witchcraft: 'Witches are people without their right minds. They make disease and spread sickness to make the living die,' and every witch must confess before all the people or alone before the Creator. The third word is Ono'ia'yi'yende, the secret poisons in little bundles named Gawennodus'hii (compelling charms), a great pile of human bodies lies dead because of this word. The fourth word is the way Gondwinias swayas, she cuts it off by abortion: the mother who administers the medicine forever cuts away her daughter's string of children, and the Creator wishes such evils to cease.
summary.zh: 四句話述說大惡，造物主為之悲傷。第一句是「瓦內加」（烈酒）：造物主造了它，賜給白人兄弟作藥，「他們卻以之作惡……造物主本不為你們而造」。第二句是「巫術」：「巫者乃失其正心之人；他們製病散瘟，令生者速死」——凡巫聞此訓示必當眾懺悔，或獨對造物主懺悔。第三句是「秘毒」——小束中的迫使咒物，因這一句話堆積如山的屍骸。第四句是「斷絕」——母親以藥物終止女兒的妊娠，永遠割斷女兒的孩子之串；造物主願此等惡行止息。

sensitivity.note: Living Haudenosaunee scripture of the Longhouse religion (Parker 1913 edition); public domain. Presented as the historical text of record; ritual confession formulas are quoted as liturgy, not instruction.

passages.text: Now the beings spoke saying, 'We must now relate our message. We will uncover the evil upon the earth and show how men spoil the laws the Great Ruler has made and thereby made him angry. The Creator made man a living creature. Four words tell a great story of wrong and the Creator is sad because of the trouble they bring, so go and tell your people. The first word is One'ga'. It seems that you never have known that this word stands for a great and monstrous evil and has reared a high mound of bones. Ga'nigohento'tha, you lose your minds and one'ga' causes it all... So now all must now say, I will use it nevermore. As long as I live, as long as the number of my days is I will never use it again. I now stop.' Furthermore they said that the Creator made one'ga' and gave it to our younger brethren, the white man, as a medicine but they use it for evil, for they drink it for other purposes than medicine and drink instead of work and idlers drink one'ga'. No, the Creator did not make it for you.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 1; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Now spoke the beings and said, 'We now speak of the second word. This makes the Creator angry. The word is Got'gon. Witches are people without their right minds. They make disease and spread sickness to make the living die. They cut short the numbered days, for the Creator has given each person a certain number of days in which to live in this world. Now this must you do: When you have told this message and the witches hear it they will confess before all the people and will say, I am doing this evil thing but now I cease it forever, as long as I live. Some witches are more evil and can not speak in public so these must come privately and confess to you, Handsome Lake, or a preacher of this Gai'wiio'. Now some are most evil and they must go far out upon an abandoned trail and there they must confess before the Creator alone.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 2; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Now the beings spoke again saying, 'This is the third word. It is a sad one and the Creator is very sad because of this third word. It seems that you have never known that a great pile of human bodies lies dead because of this word, Ono'ia'yi'yende, the niga'hos'saa', the secret poisons in little bundles named Gawennodus'hii (compelling charms). Now the Creator who made us commands that they who do this evil, when they hear this message, must stop it immediately and do it nevermore while they live upon this earth-world. It matters not how much destruction they have wrought - let them repent and not fail for fear the Creator will not accept them as his own.' Now another word.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 3-4; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: It is sad. It is the fourth word. It is the way Gondwinias swayas. Now the Creator ordained that women should bear children. Now a certain young married woman had children and suffered much. Now she is with child again and her mother wishing to prevent further sufferings designs to administer a medicine to cut off the child... Now when she does this she forever cuts away her daughter's string of children. Now it is because of such things that the Creator is sad. He created life to live and he wishes such evils to cease.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 3-4; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Spirit of the Corn Would Follow Him

region.en: Planted field at Cold Spring, Allegany Seneca country
region.zh: 阿利根尼塞內卡冷泉村的玉米田

source.work: A. C. Parker (ed.), The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913), Section 48

summary.en: When the people reviled him the prophet thought to depart to Tonawanda, that his bones might find a resting place there. The messengers came and said they would visit him more frequently, and that his life journey would be in three stages, and when he entered the third he would enter into the eternity of the New World, the land of our Creator. 'The day was bright when I went into the planted field and alone I wandered in the planted field and it was the time of the second hoeing. Suddenly a damsel appeared and threw her arms about my neck and as she clasped me she spoke saying, When you leave this earth for the new world above, it is our wish to follow you. I looked for the damsel but saw only the long leaves of corn twining round my shoulders. And then I understood that it was the spirit of the corn who had spoken, she the sustainer of life. So I replied, O spirit of the corn, follow not me but abide still upon the earth and be strong and be faithful to your purpose. Ever endure and do not fail the children of women. It is not time for you to follow for Gai'wiio' is only in its beginning.'
summary.zh: 眾人詆毀先知時，他想遷往托納萬達，使骸骨得所安息。使者前來說將更常來訪，並說他的生命之旅將分三段，入第三段時便進入「新世界」——造物主之地的永恆。「那天天色明亮，我獨行於已鋤二遍的玉米田中。忽有一位少女現身，摟住我的頸項說道：『當你離開此地上達新世界時，我們願隨你而去。』我尋那少女，卻只見長長的玉米葉纏繞我的肩頭。我這才明白，說話的正是玉米之靈，那生命的哺育者。我答道：『玉米之靈啊，不要隨我，且留守大地，剛強堅忍，莫負婦人之子。你隨我之時未到，因為長屋之教方才起始。』」

passages.text: Now it was that when the people reviled me, the proclaimer of the prophecy, the impression came to me that it would be well to depart and go to Tonawanda. In that place I had relatives and friends and thought that my bones might find a resting place there. Then the messengers came to me and said 'We understand your thoughts. We will visit you more frequently and converse with you. Wherever you go take care not to be alone. Be cautious and move secretly.' Then the messengers told me that my life journey would be in three stages and when I entered the third I would enter into the eternity of the New World, the land of our Creator.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 48; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The day was bright when I went into the planted field and alone I wandered in the planted field and it was the time of the second hoeing. Suddenly a damsel appeared and threw her arms about my neck and as she clasped me she spoke saying, 'When you leave this earth for the new world above, it is our wish to follow you.' I looked for the damsel but saw only the long leaves of corn twining round my shoulders. And then I understood that it was the spirit of the corn who had spoken, she the sustainer of life. So I replied, 'O spirit of the corn, follow not me but abide still upon the earth and be strong and be faithful to your purpose. Ever endure and do not fail the children of women. It is not time for you to follow for Gai'wiio' is only in its beginning.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 48; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Dispute in the Heaven-World: Creator and Tormentor
title.zh: 天界之爭：造物主與折磨者

region.en: The heaven-world (symbolic pin at the sky-road's start)
region.zh: 天界（象徵性定位於天路起點）

source.work: A. C. Parker (ed.), The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913), Section 49

summary.en: There is a dispute in the heaven-world between two parties - a controversy about the children of earth between the Great Ruler, the Creator, and the evil-minded spirit. 'I am the ruler of the earth because when I command I speak but once and man obeys.' 'The earth is mine for I have created it and you have helped me in no part.' The evil one answers that when he bids a child 'Pick up that stick and strike your fellow, they obey me quickly,' while they do not hear the Creator's voice. 'Truly the children are my own for they have never done evil.' So the Great Ruler resolves to send his messengers once more, and commands that hereafter his people call him Hodianok'doo' Hed'iohe', Our Creator, and the evil one Segoewa'tha, The Tormentor - 'then will the evil one know that you have discovered who he is, for it is he who will punish the wicked when they depart from this world.'
summary.zh: 天界之中兩造相爭，所爭者正是地上的孩子——一方是造物主，一方是惡靈。「我一開口命令，人便服從，故我乃大地之主。」「大地為我所造，你未助我一毫。」惡靈答道：他命令孩子拾杖擊打同伴，孩子立刻照辦；而造物主的聲音他們卻聽不見。「孩子們從未作惡，確是我的。」於是造物主決意再遣使者，並命其民此後稱他為「我們的造物主」，稱惡靈為「折磨者」——「那時惡靈便知你已識破他的本相；人離世之後，懲罰惡人的正是他。」

sensitivity.note: Longhouse scripture (Parker 1913); public domain. Parker notes it as 'a typical example of Iroquois philosophy.'

passages.text: 'There is a dispute in the heaven-world between two parties. It is a controversy about you, the children of earth. Two great beings are disputing - one is the Great Ruler, the Creator, and the other is the evil-minded spirit. You who are on earth do not know the things of heaven. Now the evil one said, I am the ruler of the earth because when I command I speak but once and man obeys. Then answered the Great Ruler, The earth is mine for I have created it and you have helped me in no part. Now the evil one answered, I do not acknowledge that you have created the earth and that I helped in no part, but I say that when I say to men, Obey me, they straightway obey, but they do not hear your voice.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 49; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Then was the Great Ruler very sad and he said, 'Once more will I send my messengers and tell them my heart and they will tell my people and thus I will redeem my own.' Then the evil one replied, 'Even so it will not be long before men transgress your commands... Verily I delight in the name Hanisse'ono. It is very true that they who love my name, though they be on the other side of the earth, will find me at their backs the moment they pronounce my name.' Now at that time the Great Ruler spoke to the four messengers saying, 'Go tell mankind that at present they must not call me Hawi'n'io', the Great Ruler, until a later time, for the Evil One calls himself the Ruler of Mankind. So now whosoever is turned into my way must say when he calls upon my name, Hodianok'doo' Hed'iohe', our Creator. So also whosoever speaks the name of the evil one must say, Segoewa'tha, The Tormentor. Then will the evil one know that you have discovered who he is, for it is he who will punish the wicked when they depart from this world.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 49; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Man Who Dishonored the Gai'wiio' and Sat in a Nest of Snakes
title.zh: 褻瀆長屋之教者與蛇巢

region.en: Cold Spring village and the swamp beyond the Allegany
region.zh: 冷泉村與阿利根尼河彼岸的沼澤

source.work: A. C. Parker (ed.), The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913), Section 47

summary.en: It happened that at a certain time a certain person did not honor Gai'wiio'. At a gathering where Gai'wiio' was being told, at Cold Spring village, a man was standing in the doorway showing disrespect to the proceedings within. The prophet was speaking, and as he said in closing 'It is finished,' the man in the doorway daini'Madi. Now that was the last. The man did not go home to his dwelling and the next day it was rumored that he was missing. A search was made and on the other side of the Allegany in a swamp two days later the man was found. He was sitting above it. He had broken branches and arranged them in the form of a nest upon which he sat devouring snakes. He was not in his right mind. They took him from his nest and soon he died.
summary.zh: 冷泉村的一次聚會上，長屋之教正在宣講；一名男子立在門口，對屋內的儀程大不敬。先知講畢說道「完畢了」，那門口的男子便發出一聲怪叫。從此再無下文。他沒有回家；次日村中傳言他失蹤了。眾人搜尋兩日，在阿利根尼河彼岸的沼澤中尋見他——他坐在折枝搭成的巢上，吞食蛇類，神志已失。眾人把他從巢中帶回，不久他便死了。

passages.text: It happened that at a certain time a certain person did not honor Gai'wiio'. At a gathering where Gai'wiio' was being told this was done. It was at Cold Spring village. A man was standing in the doorway showing disrespect to the proceedings within. The prophet was speaking and as he said in closing 'It is finished,' the man in the doorway daini'Madi. Now that was the last. The man did not go home to his dwelling and the next day it was rumored that he was missing. A search was made and on the other side of the Allegany in a swamp two days later the man was found. He was sitting above it. He had broken branches and arranged them in the form of a nest upon which he sat devouring snakes. He was not in his right mind. They took him from his nest and soon he died.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 47; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Moving Bullet: The Divination That Found the Murdered Father
title.zh: 會動的子彈：尋獲被弒之父的神判

region.en: Between Ganos' (Franklin, Pa.) and Hanenk'gaek (Oil City, Pa.)
region.zh: 賓州法蘭克林與油城之間的山地

source.work: A. C. Parker (ed.), The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913), Sections 52 and 56

summary.en: News spread that a young man had returned from the hunting grounds without his companion: 'My father is lost. I walked and searched and signalled with gun discharges hoping to find him.' Gaiant'waka said it was apparent the young man had spoken an untruth, and charged that the boy had murdered his own father. The prophet answered: 'They have not yet given me the power to see things, but this will I do. Bring a bullet, a knife, and a hatchet that the boy may look upon these things when I speak... One of these things will move though not touched and he shall be the witness.' The objects were spread on a blanket in the middle of the floor; as they watched he spoke and the bullet moved - and the prophet declared the crime was committed between Ganos' and Hanenk'gaek, where on the south side of a mountain a broken elm leans downhill, and beneath its leaves lies the father's body. The delegation went as they had been told and found the body of the father and brought it back with them.
summary.zh: 消息傳開：一青年獨自自獵場歸來，說「父親失蹤了，我走了許多天、鳴槍呼喚都尋不見」。加安特瓦卡斷言少年說謊，直指他弒父。先知答道：「他們尚未賜我看物之力，但我要如此行。取子彈、刀、斧來，讓少年在我言語時注視這些物件……其中一件雖未被觸碰卻會移動，那便是見證。」眾人把物件鋪在屋中央的毯上，圍觀之際先知開口，子彈果然移動。先知宣告：罪行發生於兩鎮之間，南山之陽一株斷榆向西傾垂，落葉之下葬著父親的屍身。使者依言前往，果然尋獲父层，攜之而歸。

passages.text: It was during the hunting season that the news spread that some one had returned from the hunting grounds without a companion. It was the young man who had returned. So they questioned him and asked where his father was. He answered, 'My father is lost. I went about searching for my father a number of days. I walked and searched and signalled with gun discharges hoping to find him. I could not find him and became weary waiting for his return.' Now Gaiant'waka when he heard this said, 'It is apparent to me that the young man has spoken the untruth.' So then they all went to the diviner of mysteries and Gaiant'waka spoke to him saying, 'It is my opinion that the boy has murdered his own father.' And the prophet answering said, 'They have not yet given me the power to see things but this will I do. Bring a bullet, a knife, and a hatchet that the boy may look upon these things when I speak and perhaps the truth will come. One of these things will move though not touched and he shall be the witness.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 56; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: So the head men did as bidden and placed the objects as directed. In the middle of the floor they spread a blanket and put the articles upon it. Then they gathered around it and watched, and as they watched he spoke and the bullet moved. Thus it happened. Then spoke Ganio'dai'io'. 'This brings the confirmation of the rumor. Truly the youth has murdered his father, and furthermore I say that the crime was committed between Ganos' and Hanenk'gaek. On the south side of a mountain, where half way up an elm is broken, leaning over on the downhill side to the west lies the body buried in the leaves of the top branches. He, the father, is buried in the leaves.' The chiefs and head-men appointed a delegation to see if all he had said were true. So they went as they had been told and found the body of the father and brought it back with them.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 56; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Gathered Host of Medicines: Speak to the Plant Before You Pluck It
title.zh: 群藥之會：採藥先與植物言語

region.en: The heaven-road vision of the assembled healing medicines
region.zh: 天路異象中群聚的療癒之藥

source.work: A. C. Parker (ed.), The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913), Section 64

summary.en: Now the messengers commanded him to give attention and he did. Then he saw a great assembly and the assembly was singing: 'The whole earth is here assembled, the whole world may come to us. We are ready.' The messengers said: 'It is very true. The beings that you saw resemble human creatures... Now the assembly is a gathered host of medicines for healing. Now let this be your ceremony when you wish to employ the medicine in a plant: First offer tobacco. Then tell the plant in gentle words what you desire of it and pluck it from the roots. It is said in the upper world that it is not right to take a plant for medicine without first talking to it. Let not one ever be taken without first speaking.'
summary.zh: 使者命他凝神觀照，他便見到大群會眾齊聲歌唱：「全地的人都在此聚會，全世界都可來到我們這裡。我們已預備好了。」使者說：「你確實看見了。你所見的靈者形貌似人……那會眾乃是醫病的群藥之聚。你若要用某株植物入藥，當行此禮：先獻菸草，再以溫言告訴它你所求，然後自根拔起。上天有言：不先與植物說話便採藥，是不義之舉。凡採必先言。」

passages.text: Now the messengers commanded him to give attention and he did. Then he saw a great assembly and the assembly was singing: 'The whole earth is here assembled, The whole world may come to us. We are ready.' Then said the messengers, 'What did you see when you gave attention?' He answered, 'I saw a great gathering of beings and the gathering was singing.' Then said the messengers, 'It is very true. The beings that you saw resemble human creatures. It is true that they are singing. Now the assembly is a gathered host of medicines for healing. Now let this be your ceremony when you wish to employ the medicine in a plant: First offer tobacco. Then tell the plant in gentle words what you desire of it and pluck it from the roots. It is said in the upper world that it is not right to take a plant for medicine without first talking to it. Let not one ever be taken without first speaking.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 64; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Sky-Road Omens: Prison House, Falling Drops, and the Veil Over All
title.zh: 天路諸兆：囚屋、懸滴與遮天之幕

region.en: The sky-road above the Buffalo Creek country
region.zh: 水牛溪之地上空的天路

source.work: A. C. Parker (ed.), The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913), Sections 86-93

summary.en: Along the sky-road the messengers halt at each omen: a strongly built house containing a pair of handcuffs, a whip and a hang-rope - the prison for those who say the white man's laws are better than the teachings of Gai'wiio'; a spired house with a path in and none out, hot within with wailing - the fate of those who embrace the belief of Bible believers; Buffalo Creek reservation honeycombed and covered with a net - 'Truly we think that this reservation will fall'; two immense drops, one red and one yellow, suspended in the eastern heavens - should one fall it would bring great calamity upon the earth, and many people would leave it; the wailing of the aged and crying of children - the substance of life going back to the Creator; an angry white man pacing with a bayonet - 'Indians must not help him'; a white house suspended in the air where the first president walks with a penny dog - for he spared the Iroquois when the king gave them up 'a thing for a sacrifice'; and a great white object slowly revolving, the Oda'eo, the veil over all, which would injure mankind should it revolve too fast - 'Now we are the regulators and watchers of the veil over all.'
summary.zh: 天路沿途，使者逐一停步示兆：一座堅固之屋，內有手銬、皮鞭與絞索——是給那些說白人律法勝過長屋之教的囚牢；一座尖頂之屋，路只進不出，屋內酷熱、哭喊不絕——是信奉《聖經》之人的歸處；水牛溪保留地如蜂巢般蛀空、又被網罩住——「這保留地必將傾覆」；東天懸著兩大滴液，一紅一黃，隨時欲墜——一滴落下，大地必遭大劫，許多人將離世；耳聞老人哀哭、孩童啼叫——那是生命的質料正回到造物主那裡；一個手持刺刀、踱步發怒的白人——「印第安人不可助他」；空中懸著一座白屋，第一任總統與小狗在廊上漫步——因國王把他們當祭品丟棄時，他說「讓他們活著，回他們自己的地方去，他們是獨立的民族」；還有一件緩緩旋轉的白色巨物——遮天之幕「奧達奧」，轉得太快便傷害人類——「我們正是遮天之幕的看管者。」

sensitivity.note: Longhouse scripture (Parker 1913); public domain. The anti-Christian polemic is quoted as the historical text, not endorsed.

passages.text: So they proceeded a short distance and again came to a halt. Then the messengers pointed out a spot and bade him watch attentively. Then he saw a house strongly built and within it he saw three different things. The first was a pair of handcuffs, the second a whip and the third a hang-rope... Then they replied, 'Truly it is a strongly built house. It is a prison. Now it is true that three things are there for punishment. How hard it is for a transgressor to see that he should be punished; yet it is the cry of the people that the laws of the white man are better than the teachings of Gai'wiio'. This frightens even the Great Spirit for he knows the punishment of those who say such things.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 86; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: So they proceeded and it was not long before they said, 'We must stop here.' Then they pointed in a certain direction and commanded him to watch. So he watched and as he did he saw a house with a spire and a path leading into the house and none out. There was no door, neither were there any windows in the house. Within was a great noise, wailing and crying, and the house was hot. Then the messengers asked him what he saw. 'You have truly seen. It is a hard matter for Indians to embrace these conditions, that is, to embrace the belief of Bible believers.' So they proceeded... 'Look downward upon the Buffalo Creek reservation.' So he looked and the place seemed honeycombed and covered with a net... Then the messengers said, 'Truly! We think that this reservation will fall.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 87-88; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: So he looked and saw two immense drops (or balls of liquid) hanging, one red and one yellow. It seemed that they were suspended only for an instant and would momentarily fall. Then the messengers replied, 'Truly you have spoken. It is so. Should one of those drops fall it would bring great calamity upon the earth. Many people would leave the earth should one drop but we are doing our utmost to prevent such an event.' So they proceeded... Now listen to the earth. So he listened and as well as he could understand he thought that he heard wailing and mourning. The sounds seemed to be the crying of children. 'It is true. What you have heard is the substance of life going back to the Creator. When this time comes there will be great misery upon the earth.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 89-90; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: He saw a house suspended there and on the veranda with a railing about it, a man walked and with him was a penny dog... the man was rejoicing and he was a white man. Then said the messengers, 'Truly you have seen. It is said that the man is the first and oldest president of the United States... Now it is said that there was once a time when the Thirteen Fires and the King were in trouble... Said the king, You have overpowered me, so now I release everything that was in my control, even these Iroquois who were my helpers. It rests with you what shall be done with them. Let them be to you a thing for a sacrifice. Then said the president, I shall let them live and go back to the places that are theirs for they are an independent people... He has ordered things that we may enjoy ourselves, as long as the sun shines and waters run.' They saw a large object revolving. It was white and moving slowly... It is that which regulates the air over the earth. It is that which we call the Oda'eo (the veil over all). It is said that it would bring great calamity should it revolve too fast... Now we are the regulators and watchers of the veil over all.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 92-93; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Sega'hedus, He Who Resurrects: The Meeting on the Sky-Road
title.zh: 復活者塞加赫杜斯：天路相遇

region.en: The sky-road toward the world beyond the great waters

source.work: A. C. Parker (ed.), The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913), Section 94

summary.en: A vision appeared unto them: they seemed to be advancing toward an approaching man, greeted each other, and he asked, 'Did you never hear your grandfathers say that once there was a certain man upon the earth across the great waters who was slain by his own people?' 'I am he,' said the man - Sega'hedus, He Who Resurrects - and he turned his palms upward and they were scarred and his feet were likewise and his breast was pierced by a spear wound, his hands and feet torn by iron nails, blood fresh upon him. 'They slew me because of their independence and unbelief. So I have gone home to shut the doors of heaven that they may not see me again until the earth passes away. Then will all the people cry to me for succor... Now let me ask how your people receive your teachings.' 'You are more successful than I, for some believe in you but none in me. I am inclined to believe that in the end it will also be so with you... Now tell your people that they will become lost when they follow the ways of the white man.'
summary.zh: 異象顯現：他們迎面遇見一位男子，相互問候。那人問道：「你可曾聽祖輩說起，大洋彼岸曾有某人被自己的族人殺害？」「我就是他」——復活者塞加赫杜斯——他翻掌向上，掌上有疤，雙足亦然，胸前有矛傷，手足被鐵釘洞穿，血猶新鮮。「他們因自大與不信而殺我。所以我回家去，把天堂的門關上，直到大地終結。那時萬民必呼求我救助……你的族人如何領受你的教導？」「你比我成功，因為有人信你，卻無人信我。但我想你的結局也會如此……告訴你的族人：隨白人之路而行，必致迷失。」

sensitivity.note: Longhouse scripture (Parker 1913); public domain. The Christian figure as seen from within Haudenosaunee theology of record.

passages.text: So they proceeded on their journey and it happened that a vision appeared unto them. They seemed to be advancing toward an approaching man. Soon they met him and passed. Now when they were a distance apart they turned and he was facing them. So they greeted each other. Then said the man, 'Sedwago'wane, I must ask you a question. Did you never hear your grandfathers say that once there was a certain man upon the earth across the great waters who was slain by his own people?' That was what he said when he spoke. Then answered Sedwago'wane, 'It is true. I have heard my grandparents say this.' Then answered the man, 'I am he.' (Sega'hedus, He Who Resurrects). And he turned his palms upward and they were scarred and his feet were likewise and his breast was pierced by a spear wound. It appeared that his hands and his feet were torn by iron nails. All this was true. It could be seen and blood was fresh upon him.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 94; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Then said the man, 'They slew me because of their independence and unbelief. So I have gone home to shut the doors of heaven that they may not see me again until the earth passes away. Then will all the people cry to me for succor, and when I come it will be in this wise: my face will be sober and I shall turn it to my people. Now let me ask how your people receive your teachings.' He answered, 'It is my opinion that half my people are inclined to believe in me.' Then answered he, 'You are more successful than I for some believe in you but none in me. I am inclined to believe that in the end it will also be so with you. Now it is rumored that you are but a talker with spirits. Now it is true that I am a spirit and the one of him who was murdered. Now tell your people that they will become lost when they follow the ways of the white man.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 94; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: Sagoyewatha Carrying Dirt: Red Jacket's Doom on the Sky-Road
title.zh: 紅夾克負土：天路上的報應

region.en: The broad road of the sky-journey, toward the setting sun
region.zh: 天路上通往日落方向的寬路

source.work: A. C. Parker (ed.), The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913), Section 95

summary.en: The messengers pointed out a certain spot and said, 'Watch attentively,' and beheld a man carrying loads of dirt and depositing them in a certain spot. He carried the earth in a wheelbarrow and his task was a hard one. Then he knew that the name of the man was Sagoyewat'ha, a chief. 'You have spoken truly. Sagoyewat'ha is the name of the man who carries the dirt. It is true that his work is laborious and this is for a punishment for he was the one who first gave his consent to the sale of Indian reservations. It is said that there is hardship for those who part with their lands for money or trade. So now you have seen the doom of those who repent not. Their eternity will be one of punishment.'
summary.zh: 使者指向某處說「用心看」——他見一人推著獨輪車運土、傾倒於一處，勞苦不堪。他認出那人的名字是酋長薩戈耶瓦塔（紅夾克）。「你說得不錯。運土者正是薩戈耶瓦塔。他的勞苦是懲罰——因為他第一個同意出賣印第安人的保留地。凡為金錢交易放棄土地者必有苦難。你已看見不悔改者的下場：他們的永恆就是刑罰。」

sensitivity.note: Longhouse scripture (Parker 1913); public domain. Parker notes the Gai'wiio' followers mention Red Jacket's name 'with contempt' to this day.

passages.text: So they proceeded on their journey and had not gone far when they came to a halt. Then the messengers pointed out a certain spot and said, 'Watch attentively,' and beheld a man carrying loads of dirt and depositing them in a certain spot. He carried the earth in a wheelbarrow and his task was a hard one. Then he knew that the name of the man was Sagoyewat'ha, a chief. Then asked the messengers, 'What did you see?' He answered, 'I beheld a man carrying dirt in a wheelbarrow and that man had a laborious task. His name was Sagoyewat'ha, a chief.' Then answered the messengers, 'You have spoken truly. Sagoyewat'ha is the name of the man who carries the dirt. It is true that his work is laborious and this is for a punishment for he was the one who first gave his consent to the sale of Indian reservations. It is said that there is hardship for those who part with their lands for money or trade. So now you have seen the doom of those who repent not. Their eternity will be one of punishment.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 95; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Forks of the Great Road: Narrow and Rough
title.zh: 大路的岔口：窄路與崎路

region.en: The forks of the sky-road where the spirits of the dead are divided

source.work: A. C. Parker (ed.), The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913), Section 96

summary.en: They saw a crowd on both sides of the road, and when they came to where it was they saw that they were at the forks of the road. One road, on the right, was a narrow one and the tracks upon it were mostly those of children and all were pointed in one direction; few adults had their tracks on this road, the road rough and wide. As they watched they saw a woman approaching the forks from behind them. The man on the left shouted, 'To this side'; the man on the right answered, 'Not so. This woman has done her whole duty. She has truly repented' - for in her earth-life she repented and was faithful to her promises, and this is all that is required, and she will walk upon the narrow road. 'The woman has lived a repented life for three days and has entered into the happy eternity... Three times we assist every one who believes to continue in the faith of the Gai'wiio'. At this division in the great road we guide the spirits of the earth into Tain'tciade (heaven land). At the forks of the road the spirits of the dead are divided. The narrow road leads to the pleasant lands of the Creator and the wide and rough road leads to the great lodge of the punisher.'
summary.zh: 他們見路之兩旁聚著人群——原來已到大路的岔口。右邊是窄路，路上的足跡多半是孩子的，同指一個方向；成人寥寥。左邊的路寬而崎嶇。這時一位女子從身後走到岔口。左邊的人喊道「走這邊」；右邊的人答：「不對。這女子已盡了本分，真心悔改了。」——她在世時悔改並守其諾言，這便足夠，她將行在窄路上。「她悔改了三日便進入幸福的永恆。凡信者，我們三次扶助他持守長屋之教。在這大路的岔口，我們把地上亡者之靈引入天土。窄路通往造物主的樂土，寬而崎嶇的路通往刑罰者的大屋。」

passages.text: Now again they took up their journey and had not traveled far when they saw a crowd on both sides of the road. And when they came to where it was they saw that they were at the forks of the road. One road, on the right, was a narrow one and the tracks upon it were mostly those of children and all were pointed in one direction. Few adults had their tracks on this road, the road rough and wide. Now as they watched they saw a woman approaching the forks of the road from behind them.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 96; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: She came to where the road divided and as she halted before the roads a man who stood to the left shouted, 'To this side.' (Now the road of the wicked is owa'etga', a rough road.) Then the man on the right said, 'Not so. This woman has done her whole duty. She has truly repented.' Then answered the man on the left, 'You are wrong, for her repentance has been of short duration and so of slight effect.' But the man on the right replied, 'Truly in her earth-life she repented and was faithful to her promises. This is all that is required and she will walk upon the narrow road.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 96; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Now one of the messengers turned to him and said, 'The woman has lived a repented life for three days and has entered into the happy eternity. It was not an easy matter for her to do so of herself, but we, the messengers, have plead before the Creator and he has heard us. Three times we assist every one who believes to continue in the faith of the Gai'wiio'. At this division in the great road we guide the spirits of the earth into Tain'tciade (heaven land). At the forks of the road the spirits of the dead are divided. The narrow road leads to the pleasant lands of the Creator and the wide and rough road leads to the great lodge of the punisher.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 96; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The House of the Punisher: Molten Drink, the Cauldron, and Hot Cards
title.zh: 刑罰者之屋：熔漿之飲、沸釜與滾燙的紙牌

region.en: The great iron lodge at the end of the rough road
region.zh: 崎嶇之路盡頭的鐵鑄大屋

source.work: A. C. Parker (ed.), The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913), Sections 98-109

summary.en: Soon they began to inhale heated air and heard the far away echoes of mournful cries borne on the blasts of the hot wind. They approached a great lodge constructed of iron highly heated and allowed to cool, hot vapor rising from the fire pits; a being walked about as if master of the lodge, at times horns shot out from his forehead, at times a cloven foot appeared and at times a tail was visible - the punisher, who torments those who refused the words of Gai'wiio'. He compelled the drunkard to warm himself with molten metal - 'Now warm yourself again as was your custom while on the earth for you loved hot drink'; plunged the witch into a boiling cauldron - 'O, it is too hot! I should have an interval in which to cool myself!' 'Thou art not one-minded' - and thrust her back until her bones rattled to the bottom; forced the wife-beater to beat an image heated hot with fire; made the quarreling couple dispute until flames shot from their mouths; thrust the red-hot object into the immoral woman; forced the violinist to rub a bar of hot iron upon his arm for strings; and dealt to the card-players a pack of red hot iron cards until their flesh fell off - such are the punishments of those who will not believe in Gai'wiio'.
summary.zh: 熱風撲面，哀哭隨風隱隱傳來。他們走近一座鐵鑄的大屋——鐵被燒得極熱又冷卻成形，火坑中熱氣蒸騰。一個靈者在屋中踱步如主人：額上時時迸出角、時時現出分蹄、時時露出尾巴——這就是刑罰者，凡在世上拒絕長屋之教者皆受其折磨。他強令酒徒喝下熔化的金屬——「你在世上愛喝燙的，如今再暖一暖自己」；把巫婆按進沸釜——「太燙了！總該讓我涼一涼！」「你心不專一」——又按回去，直到她的骨頭咯咯沉底；逼打妻者赤手毆打燒紅的人偶；令爭吵不休的夫妻對辯，直到口噴火焰；把燒紅之物塞入淫婦體內；令琴師以燒紅的鐵條在臂上「拉琴」；發給賭徒一副燒紅的鐵紙牌，直到他們的肉一片片脫落——凡不信長屋之教者，便是如此下場。

sensitivity.note: Longhouse scripture (Parker 1913); public domain. Parker notes the prophet's devil imagery is borrowed from transatlantic sources.

passages.text: Now, strange, this was true; some great force seemed pushing them onward toward the house of the punisher. Soon they began to inhale heated air and soon they heard the far away echoes of mournful cries borne on the blasts of the hot wind. At times the air was suffocating and the cries of the doomed were distressing... They approached a great lodge. It seemed constructed of iron that had been highly heated and allowed to cool. Within the building hot vapor was rising from the fire pits... one of the beings took from his bosom a crystal and pointed it at the lodge: as he came near the lodge arose to the height of the man so powerful was the crystal.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 98-99; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: Now as they looked they saw a being walking about as if he were the master of the lodge. He seemed continually distorting himself. At times horns shot out from his forehead, at times a cloven foot appeared and at times a tail was visible. Then said the four messengers to Ganio'dai'io', 'That being is the punisher. It is he who torments those who have refused the words of Gai'wiio' when they heard them on the earth.' In a loud voice the punisher cried to a certain person saying, 'Come hither.' The punisher held a drinking vessel in his hand and within it was molten metal and thrusting it in the hands of the man he had called he said, 'Now warm yourself again as was your custom while on the earth for you loved hot drink.' Now the man pleaded but the punisher compelled him to swallow the molten metal. Then the man screamed in a loud voice and fell prone upon the ground with vapor steaming from his throat.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 101-102; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: And straightway a woman came to where he stood. Then he grabbed her and forced her body into a great cauldron filled with a boiling liquid... Suddenly she shot to the surface crying in a strange voice like some unknown animal: 'O, it is too hot! I should have an interval in which to cool myself!' Answered the punisher, 'Thou art not one-minded,' and jerking her out he flung her on one side. But the woman screeched in agony, 'O, it is too cold!' and her complaint was continuous... Then the punisher thrust her back into the boiling cauldron and immediately her bones rattled to the bottom. Such was the punishment given by the keeper of the house of torment... This is the punishment given those who practice witchcraft. The woman whom you saw will suffer two deaths in this place and when her body is reduced to dust the punisher will gather them up again and conjure the dust back into a living body and continue his sport.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Section 103; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: The master of the house called out the names of two persons, saying, 'Come here, my nephews,' and straightway they stood before him. Then said he, 'Commence an argument, you two, for you are the man and wife who in your earth-life were wont to quarrel continually, so quarrel again!' Then when he saw that the people were reluctant he compelled them to argue. Then they disputed until their eyes bulged from their heads, their tongues lolled out and flames of fire shot from ganii'shoo'. The punisher called out a certain woman's name saying, 'Come to me, my niece,' and straightway she came. 'It was once your delight, gaknowe'haat.' As he said this he lifted up an object from a pile and thrust it within her... Then she cried aloud in agony and she fell with steam issuing from her body. Now there were three piles of ga'naa', the first white, the second red and the third black... 'Now, nephew, play your violin as was once your delight.' The punisher handed the man a bar of hot iron and forced him to rub it upon his arm... Then he handed them what seemed a pack of red hot iron cards. Then he forced the two to sit down facing each other and compelled them to shuffle the cards and as they did flames spurted out from between them... This is the punishment meted out to those who handle cards and repent not.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 106-109; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

title.en: The Heaven-Road: The Spring, the White Dog, and the House Prepared
title.zh: 天路樂土：活泉、白犬與備好的居所

region.en: The narrow road into Tain'tciade, the heaven land

source.work: A. C. Parker (ed.), The Code of Handsome Lake, the Seneca Prophet (1913), Sections 112-118

summary.en: Then they went out upon the narrow road and had not gone far upon it when a far more brilliant light appeared, and they smelled the fragrant odors of the flowers along the road; delicious looking fruits were growing on the wayside and every kind of bird flew in the air above them. They came to the Spring, a place for rest, the most beautiful and clear fount of water; one of the four drew a bottle from his bosom and dipped it in the spring - 'Truly it is enough. If it lacks, there is still the spring and the vessel may be refilled.' On the road a dog came toward them, wagging its tail, his own dog as it appeared when he had decorated it for the sacrifice in the New Year's ceremony - 'This thing attests to the value of our thanksgiving to the Creator.' Children came - the daughter of Gaiant'waka and his own infant son, led by a fourth person to testify that those of the lower world when they pass away come hither; and a commanding voice called the people to the great feather dance - Joi'se, his friend, who had been faithful and good. 'We have arrived at the point where you must return. Here there is a house prepared for your eternal abode but should you now enter a room you could never go back to the earth-world.'
summary.zh: 轉上窄路不久，更明亮的光顯現，路旁花香撲鼻；甘美的果實結在道旁，百鳥飛鳴於頭頂。他們來到「活泉」——歇腳之地，水色澄澈可愛；四使者之一自懷中取瓶汲泉——「夠了；若不夠，泉仍在，瓶可再汲。」路上有犬搖尾相迎，正是他新年祭時裝扮過的那隻白犬——「這正證明我們向造物主獻祭之功。」孩子們迎面而來——加安特瓦卡的女兒與先知的幼子，由第四人引領，見證下界亡者歸此；遠處一聲令下召集眾人行大神羽舞——那是他忠善的朋友喬伊塞，在天土仍如生前為首領。「你該回程了。此處已備下你永居的屋子；但若此時入室，你便永不能再回地上世界。」

passages.text: Then they went out upon the narrow road and had not gone far upon it when a far more brilliant light appeared. It was then that they smelled the fragrant odors of the flowers along the road. Delicious looking fruits were growing on the wayside and every kind of bird flew in the air above them. The most marvelous and beautiful things were on every hand. And all these things were on the heaven road. So they continued on their journey and after a short time they came to a hall. Then spoke the messengers. 'This place is called the spring and it is a place for rest.' Then behold he saw the spring and he thought that he had never seen so beautiful and clear a fount of water...
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 112-113; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: One of the four drew a bottle from his bosom, so it seemed and it was, and dipped it in the spring. Then he said, 'You must partake first,' and so he took it, but when he looked at it he thought it was not enough. And when he had said this the messengers looked at one another and smiled and one said, 'Truly it is enough. If it lacks, there is still the spring and the vessel may be refilled.' So all took and drank and all the drink that all wished was in the bottle.
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 112-113; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: So then they proceeded on their journey and had gone but a short way when they saw someone coming toward them... Then he saw it was a dog and when they met, the dog began to wag its tail and sprang upon him. Then he recognized the animal as his own dog and it appeared just as it had when he had decorated it for the sacrifice in the New Year's ceremony. Then said the four, 'This thing attests to the value of our thanksgiving to the Creator.' So they took up their journey again and in a short time came to a halt. In the distance before them a man appeared to be coming... guiding two others, one on either side of him... one was the daughter of Gaiant'waka and it appeared that she was a large child. With her was his own son, an infant... Now moreover a fourth person was leading them all. Now that person spoke and said, 'I brought them with me to testify to the truth that those of the lower world when they pass away come hither.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 114-116; not verbatim (OCR modernized).

passages.text: There was a more brilliant light and as they stood suddenly they heard the echo of a commanding voice calling the people together for the performance of the great feather dance... He answered, 'I heard the commanding voice of Joi'se calling the people to celebrate the great feather dance.' Then replied the four messengers, 'Verily, Joi'se, your friend is he who calls. He it was who was faithful and good and when he passed away in the lands of the Creator he continued as on the earth.' So they took up their journey again and after a ways the four messengers said, 'We have arrived at the point where you must return. Here there is a house prepared for your eternal abode but should you now enter a room you could never go back to the earth-world.'
passages.note: Verbatim from Parker 1913, Sections 117-118; not verbatim (OCR modernized).
